newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters' party blamed as NZ govt gets thumbs-down.
newsitem.headline: Peters' party blamed as NZ govt gets thumbs-down.

text.p: If there was supposed to be a honeymoon period for New Zealand's coalition government, someone forgot to tell the voters.

Just 100 days after the centre-right government was formed, its approval rating has plummeted amid scandal and controversy. A nationwide survey released on Friday showed 68 percent were not satisfied with its performance.
Junior coalition partner New Zealand First and its charismatic Maori leader, Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, are getting the blame.
Peters, once the country's top-rating politician, was preferred prime minister of only 3.1 percent of the survey conducted by the Waikato University's research unit.

NZ First's support peaked at 30 percent a year ago after attacks on immigration levels, free-market economic reforms and foreign investment. It won 13 percent of the vote in the October 1996 election, but fell to 5.3 percent in the latest survey.
"You can't cry dirty pool (foul) and accuse other people. It's all self-inflicted," said Victoria University political scientist Rod Alley.
The longest-running crisis has been over funding of a Maori language television station.

In February it was revealed that NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan, a former director and presenter at the station, spent thousands of dollars of its money on expensive clothes, including NZ$89 (US$61) underpants, weeks before the election.
The spotlight shifted to Peters himself this month after a late-night altercation in a corridor of parliament, where a senior politician alleges he assaulted another MP.
Peters denied any assault but apologised for the incident. In a television interview, he admitted having a drink before the fracas but denied any "drinking problem".
Peters, a lawyer of Maori and Scottish descent, became kingmaker after October's election left him holding the balance of power between the conservative National party and Labour.

After arduous negotiations, he forged a deal with National and secured the plum job of Treasurer under Prime Minister Jim Bolger. But for three months Peters has avoided interviews, contributing to media speculation he is unsure of himself.
Citing other commitments, he has pulled out of a major trip to meet overseas investors next month and asked Finance Minister Bill Birch to take his place.

At the same time, Peters has performed a radical policy shift. Attacks on the high New Zealand dollar, a keynote of his rhetoric before the election, have been relaced by an acceptance of the market's judgment.

Calls to reduce immigration and overseas investment and to end New Zealand's "monetarist experiment" have been replaced with a conservative message of fiscal prudence and self-reliance for welfare beneficiaries.
The opposition has dubbed him a "Treasury poodle" and Labour has described his first 100 days as "characterised by crisis, cock-up and mismanagement".
Auckland political scientist Helena Catt believes Peters lacks experienced heads around him.
"Winston has got where he wants to be, but he hasn't got the support group around him to keep him there," she said.

Some of the decline in popularity appears to reflect opposition from NZ First supporters who favoured a coalition with Labour. "Some are just unhappy because the wrong coalition deal was done," Catt said.
Stern tests lie ahead for Peters in the form of a rising current account deficit and a referendum on the future of pension provisions.
The question is, can the coalition survive?

The small free-market Act party has called NZ First a "rogue populist party", and has declared political war on it. It would be well-placed to form a new coalition should NZ First disintegrate or fall from favour with National.

Alley said NZ First was being squeezed between National and Act on the right, and Labour and the left-wing Alliance on the left. Its long-term prospects, even among its strong Maori support base, were problematic.
"The attacks on the news media and the brash new image is wearing off. There is no substitute for just knuckling down and doing the job in the constituency. The electorate is pretty sceptical now."
But National, in power since 1990, has successfully quarantined itself from the problems of its coalition partner.
Its support has strengthened to 38.6 percent from 34 percent at the election. Support for the opposition Labour Party has jumped level with National.
"Everyone is happy except NZ First," said Catt.
"This is exactly what National wanted. They have given NZ First enough rope to hang themselves and they are doing it."
